To loiter means to stand, wait, or hang around somewhere for no clear or obvious reason, often for an uncomfortably long amount of time. When someone loiters, they are not going anywhere, not doing anything productive, and they have no visible purpose for being exactly where they are. They are simply... lingering there.

Understanding "loiter" is not just about what the person is doing physically — it's about how that behavior looks to others. The word carries a distinctly negative or suspicious tone. A loiterer's presence in a place feels purposeless, out of place, or unwanted.

Here's a useful contrast: if you are standing outside a café and you are clearly looking at your phone, waiting for a friend, no one would describe you as loitering. But if you are just standing around aimlessly near an entrance, not going anywhere, not clearly waiting for anything, for a long stretch of time — that is loitering.

The key ingredient is the absence of any obvious, legitimate reason to be there.

The word has two closely related meanings, and both share the same core idea of purposeless time-wasting:

1. To linger in a public place with no clear purpose — This is the most common use. The person is physically present but has no good reason to be there.

The teenagers loitered outside the convenience store for hours.
Security cameras caught a man loitering near the back entrance of the building.

2. To move somewhere very slowly, stopping frequently and wasting time along the way — Here, the idea is that someone is delaying getting to where they're supposed to be. They're dragging their feet, pausing unnecessarily, and taking far longer than they should.

Stop loitering on your way home from school and come back immediately.
She loitered through the museum hallways, barely making it to the exit before closing time.

Both meanings share a common thread: time is being wasted, and nothing meaningful is happening.
Why It Often Sounds Suspicious or Accusatory

Loitering is almost always described from the perspective of an observer who finds the loiterer's presence concerning, annoying, or suspicious. The word implies that the person is taking up space in a public area — a sidewalk, a parking lot, a shop entrance, a street corner — without any justification. This makes "loiter" a word that is frequently used by authority figures: shop owners, security guards, police officers, and parents.

This is different from simply resting or taking a break. Someone sitting on a park bench and enjoying the weather is not loitering. Someone slouching near the back of a store, not shopping, not leaving, just being there for an extended time — that person is loitering.

This word has an important legal dimension. In many countries and cities, loitering is a minor legal offense. Signs reading "No Loitering" are common outside shops, malls, schools, transit stations, and public buildings. These signs exist to prevent people from gathering without a purpose in a way that makes others uncomfortable or disrupts normal activity.

Police officers have the authority to approach someone loitering and ask them to move along, or even to issue a warning or fine in places where it is specifically prohibited by law.

Loitering (present participle and noun form): Loitering is strictly prohibited on these premises.

Loitered (past tense): He loitered outside the building for nearly an hour before someone called security.

Loiterer (noun — a person who loiters): The shop owner confronted the loiterer and told him to leave.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Linger — Also means to stay somewhere longer than expected, but "linger" is neutral or even pleasant. You linger over a delicious meal. You linger in a beautiful place because you don't want to leave. Loitering is almost always viewed negatively. Lingering is not.

Dawdle — To move very slowly and waste time, much like the second meaning of loiter. However, "dawdle" focuses purely on slowness of movement and is most often used casually (especially with children). It does not carry the suspicious or threatening undertone that loitering can.

Lurk — To wait somewhere in a hidden or secretive way. This is darker and more sinister than loitering. A lurker is concealing themselves and watching. A loiterer is visible but aimless. Lurking implies intent; loitering implies absence of any visible intent.

Hang around / Hang about — These informal phrases carry essentially the same meaning as loiter, but are casual and carry no negative weight. You'd tell a friend "let's hang around here for a bit" without any accusation. "Loiter" sounds far more formal and far more judgmental.

Idle — To spend time doing nothing. However, "idle" is a broader word used in many contexts (an engine can idle; you can idle your life away). Loitering is specifically about being physically present in a particular place with no clear purpose.

• A group of young men loitered at the corner of the street, making shopkeepers nervous.
  • The security guard asked the man who had been loitering near the entrance for the past hour to leave.
  • "No loitering — violators will be removed from the premises."
  • She pretended to look at the noticeboard while actually loitering close enough to eavesdrop on the conversation.
  • The boys loitered after school instead of going home, killing time with nowhere to be.
One Image to Remember It Forever

Picture a person standing alone outside a closed shop at night — hands in pockets, not on the phone, not waiting for a ride, not looking at anything in particular, not going anywhere. Just... there. That is loitering. The place doesn't want them. They have no reason to be there. And yet, they remain.

That purposeless, suspicious, unwelcome lingering — that is the heart of what "loiter" means.
